title: Trump H-1B Fee Fight Heads to a Showdown Over Congress's Authority
excerpt: Judges in Massachusetts and California have ruled the $100,000 fee amounts to a tax only Congress can impose; the administration has responded with a new $103,265 rulemaking that 22 states oppose.
body:
• The legal war over the Trump administration's $100,000 H-1B fee has become a fight over Congress's exclusive taxing power: judges in Massachusetts and California have ruled the president cannot levy what amounts to a tax without Congress.
  • On September 30, 2026, a federal court in California halted the fee's implementation memos in Global Nurse Force v. Trump; on June 8, Judge Leo Sorokin in Boston vacated the fee outright, calling it an unauthorized tax.
  • The administration has regrouped: on August 25, DHS proposed a new $103,265 fee on cap-subject H-1B petitions through formal rulemaking — the public comment period closed September 24, with 22 attorneys general opposing.
  • What it means for you: no $100,000 fee is being collected right now — courts have blocked it. The next risk point is the final rule on the $103,265 fee; the fee targets new petitions for workers abroad, not renewals by people already in the US. Watch for the rule's publication, not rumors.

The Trump administration's $100,000 H-1B fee — which effectively froze skilled-worker hiring at hospitals, universities and schools — has become something larger than an immigration fight. It is now a constitutional showdown over who sets the price of coming to America: the president, or Congress.

The Congress-authority argument

The administration defended the fee under the Immigration and Nationality Act's entry-restriction authority, which gives the president broad power to limit who enters the United States. But judges have refused to let that authority do the levying. In June 2026, the US District Court for the District of Massachusetts set aside the policy, concluding the payment "was not a penalty but a tax" — and that the president lacked congressional authorization to impose it, since Congress alone holds the taxing power.

That reasoning gained force from the Supreme Court's February 2026 decision in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, which overturned the administration's global tariff regime 6-3 on the same principle: only Congress can tax. Plaintiffs led by California-based nurse recruiting firm Global Nurse Force argued the INA does not allow the president to upend visa programs and fee regimes designed by lawmakers — and a federal court in the Northern District of California agreed on September 30, halting the implementation memos in Global Nurse Force v. Trump (No. 4:25-cv-08454).

"No president can rewrite immigration policy with the stroke of a pen. The administration tried to financially punish companies with an arbitrary, unauthorized, and deeply harmful $100,000 fee imposed without Congress."

— Steve Bressler, senior legal advisor at Democracy Forward, which represents the plaintiffs

"This case may have only involved a single fee on a single visa category, but Judge Sorokin recognized that, at its core, it was a question about whether Congress or the Executive Branch sets immigration policy," said Lynden Melmed, a partner at business immigration firm BAL and former chief counsel at US Citizenship and Immigration Services, in comments to Bloomberg Law.

The administration's second attempt

Blocked by proclamation, the White House switched vehicles. On August 25, the Department of Homeland Security filed a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that would establish a $103,265 fee on every H-1B petition drawn from the annual 85,000-worker cap, this time through the standard regulatory process — citing INA provisions on recovering adjudication costs. The math is the giveaway, critics say: DHS spread a projected $8.78 billion in costs across 85,000 assumed petitions, a revenue target rather than an adjudication cost, with proceeds flowing to six agencies, several with no role in processing an individual petition.

The 30-day comment period closed September 24, and the opposition was heavyweight: a coalition of 22 attorneys general — California, Virginia, Massachusetts, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia — filed a formal comment letter on September 26 calling the rule an unlawful tax requiring congressional approval.

Diaspora angle

Indian nationals are historically the largest beneficiaries of the H-1B program, and the fee was priced to do exactly what it did: the policy effectively blocked H-1B hiring at hospitals, research universities, churches and K-12 schools, and contributed to a steep drop in entries for this spring's annual lottery. The practical guidance for Indian professionals: no six-figure fee is collectible today — both the proclamation and its memos are blocked — but the rulemaking track means the question is dormant, not dead. Anyone weighing a job offer tied to a new H-1B petition should ask their employer's counsel about the $103,265 proposed rule's timeline, not assume the old fee is gone for good.

What's next

A circuit split is forming: a D.C. district court reached the opposite conclusion on the fee, while the US Chamber of Commerce's challenge is pending at the D.C. Circuit. USCIS must now review the comments on the $103,265 rule, and a final rule — subject to executive-branch review and near-certain litigation — could set up the Supreme Court showdown the constitutional question has been pointing toward all along.
